source.title: GAN D ISSECTION : V ISUALIZING AND U NDERSTANDING G ENERATIVE A DVERSARIAL N ETWORKS
source.authors: David Bau; Jun-Yan Zhu; Hendrik Strobelt; Bo-Lei Zhou; J. Tenenbaum; W. Freeman; A. Torralba

record.tranche_reason: Tests interpretability across architecture variants and layers in generative vision models, an extension of the claim’s discussion of interpretable neurons and vision-model architecture.
record.gate_note: The paper reports other unit interventions, artifact-removal results, and image-quality metrics, but those do not test the claim versions here. Figure 7’s architecture comparison and the paper’s layer and human-evaluation results bear on V4. The training-checkpoint trend is recorded separately as a related finding not covered by a version.
record.test_reason: In Progressive GAN generators (a new setting), the study compares interpretable-unit counts across architecture variants. It also shows that the measured count depends on the labelling tool. Both bear on V4's claim that architecture and tools, not capacity, set the interpretable share.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors find many GAN units interpretable as object, part or material detectors with causal effects on output. Architecture choices that improve quality also increase interpretable units. Interpretability varies by layer, with late layers dominated by textures and colours. The segmenter misses abstract concepts such as letterboxing, and better segmenters should identify more units.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses segmentation-based network dissection and interventions on Progressive GAN featuremaps, rather than auditing language-model neuron poles or testing explanations by predicting held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured unit patterns vary by layer and GAN architecture. The paper also reports changing counts and average IoU across training checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: In a bedroom Progressive GAN, layer4 object units rise from 27 to 95 and average IoU from 0.045 to 0.085 across training checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretable units emerge and sharpen over training in GAN generators.

fits_no_version.finding: In the living-room GAN, interpretable object-unit diversity peaks at layers 4–6, and later layers are dominated by textures and colours.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The kind of unit semantics varies systematically with generator depth.

record.problems: The architecture comparison concerns Progressive GANs and does not test the stated InceptionV1 estimates. Human evaluation of segmentation-based labels is reported for one living-room model; some human-consistent units are not confidently labeled, and some labels are inaccurate. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported interventions and artifact-quality results (including Table 1, Table 2, Figures 4, 9–13, and 17) do not measure V4’s interpretability share or architecture/tool claims. Figure 18 checkpoint results are retained as fits_no_version rows.

untested.parts: No language models, MoE, or scale.
No InceptionV1 cat/car neuron or pose analysis.
Untested: classifiers or InceptionV1-sized models, the 5%→99% estimates, and regularization as a separate factor. It is also not shown that messy late-layer units are caused by architecture or tools.
No attribution graphs or circuit reconstruction.
No held-out activation prediction of explanations.

missing.what: Figure 7 totals of interpretable units and SWD for each variant, roughly 167, 189 and 226 units with SWD 7.60, 6.48 and 4.01. The figure text is garbled, so these readings are approximate. Authors note interpretable units rise as quality improves.
WGAN-GP bedroom dissection: 172 interpretable units, and 124 after filtering unrealistic units (FID<55). This shows the segmenter is confused by unrealistic images in older architectures.

record.verdict_notes: The architecture comparison is confounded: variants that raise unit counts also improve realism. S-6.3 shows the segmentation-based measure itself degrades on unrealistic images, so part of the rise may reflect the tool working better rather than cleaner units. The setting is GAN generators, not classifiers, hence T3. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or neuron-pole share is measured.
No language models, dense-versus-MoE comparison, or trillion-parameter scale is studied.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or pose interpretation is examined.

The paper studies Progressive GANs, not InceptionV1-sized classifiers; it does not estimate the proposed 5%–99% range or establish that architecture, regularization, and tool quality explain all messy late-layer units.
No attribution graphs or large language model behavior reconstruction are evaluated.
The paper does not test explanations against held-out activation-prediction examples.
The paper does not score language-model neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

Fig 7 is the bedroom layer4 model; only the figure gives counts (167/189/226 interpretable units). The human eval covers one living-room model, and each architecture variant is a single run. The text gives no venue; from outside knowledge (not this text), this paper is ICLR 2019, not 2018.
